cards.front: What is the fundamental condition for two matrices $A$ and $B$ to be added or subtracted?
cards.back: They must have the **same dimensions** (i.e., the same number of rows and the same number of columns). If $A$ is an $m \times n$ matrix, $B$ must also be an $m \times n$ matrix.

cards.front: Define matrix addition $A+B$ for $A=[a_{ij}]$ and $B=[b_{ij}]$ of the same dimensions.
cards.back: The sum $C = A+B$ is a matrix $C=[c_{ij}]$ where each element $c_{ij}$ is the sum of the corresponding elements from $A$ and $B$. That is, $c_{ij} = a_{ij} + b_{ij}$.

cards.front: Define matrix subtraction $A-B$ for $A=[a_{ij}]$ and $B=[b_{ij}]$ of the same dimensions.
cards.back: The difference $C = A-B$ is a matrix $C=[c_{ij}]$ where each element $c_{ij}$ is the difference of the corresponding elements from $A$ and $B$. That is, $c_{ij} = a_{ij} - b_{ij}$. Alternatively, $A-B = A + (-1)B$.

cards.front: Prove that matrix addition is commutative, i.e., $A+B = B+A$, for matrices $A$ and $B$ of the same dimensions.
cards.back:
Let $A=[a_{ij}]$ and $B=[b_{ij}]$.
The $(i,j)$-th element of $A+B$ is $a_{ij} + b_{ij}$.
The $(i,j)$-th element of $B+A$ is $b_{ij} + a_{ij}$.
Since addition of real (or complex) numbers is commutative, $a_{ij} + b_{ij} = b_{ij} + a_{ij}$ for all $i,j$.
As all corresponding elements are equal, $A+B = B+A$.

cards.front: What is the additive identity matrix for an $m \times n$ matrix $A$?
cards.back: The additive identity matrix is the $m \times n$ **zero matrix**, denoted $0_{m \times n}$ (or simply $0$), where all its elements are zero. For any matrix $A$, $A + 0 = 0 + A = A$.

cards.front: Explain why matrix addition/subtraction is undefined if matrices have different dimensions, e.g., $A$ is $2 \times 3$ and $B$ is $2 \times 2$.
cards.back: Matrix addition/subtraction is defined element-wise. This means you combine elements at the exact same row and column position. If matrices have different dimensions, there will be elements in one matrix that do not have a corresponding element in the other. For example, $A_{13}$ (element in row 1, col 3 of $A$) has no counterpart in $B$ if $B$ is $2 \times 2$. This makes a consistent element-wise operation impossible.
